title: First Dance in Kendo — A Beginner's Guide
subtitle: 6 sources · 2026-10-11 14:20

blocks.text: Answer

Your first dance in kendo is Nihon Kendo Kata no. 1 - a partnered routine for two dancers, a leader (uchidachi) and a follower (shidachi), performed to a count of eight. Beginners can learn the whole routine in four to six sessions. Start with suriashi, the gliding step every figure is built on, keep your shinai in frame, and rehearse at a slow tempo of about 60 beats per minute.
1. Leading and following

The uchidachi leads: they set the tempo, take the first step and invite each figure. The shidachi follows - and, as in any partner dance, never anticipates the lead [2].

The connection runs through the tips of the shinai, crossed about ten centimetres apart. This is kendo's closed hold: if the tips drift apart, the couple has lost the frame.
2. Suriashi - the basic step

• Count 1 - glide the right foot forward, heel just off the floor
• Count 2 - the left foot follows, closing to the starting distance
• Counts 3-4 - the same again
• Counts 5-8 - the same pattern, travelling backward

Never cross the feet, and never let the left heel touch the floor: it stays lifted for the entire routine [1] [5].

blocks.caption: kata 1 floor plan - three steps in, the cut on 4, out on 5 to 8

blocks.text: 3. The routine, figure by figure

• The bow (rei) - both partners, counts 1-2
• Sonkyo - the crouching dip, counts 3-4
• The frame (kamae) - the leader in jodan, shinai raised; the follower in chudan
• The approach - three suriashi steps in, on counts 1-2-3
• The cut - the leader strikes men on count 4; the follower steps back out of it and answers on the same count
• Zanshin - the held final pose, two full counts

The audience should not applaud until zanshin is released [3] [6].
4. Rhythm and tempo

Kata is danced to silence, but it has a strict pulse. Count in eights, like a salsa phrase, and keep the count in your head rather than your feet. The kiai is the accent on the downbeat - 'Yah!' for the leader, 'Toh!' for the follower - and never on the off-beat [4]. Most beginners rush the approach: around 60 BPM is right for a first dance.
5. Grading levels

• 1st kyu - the routine, with correct footwork
• Shodan - the routine in time with your partner
• Nidan - styling and presence
• Sandan and above - musicality: the pause before the cut becomes part of the performance

A first dance needs 1st kyu footwork. Leave the advanced styling for your second dance [3].
6. Performance tips for your first dance

• Keep eye contact with your partner for the whole routine - in kata, the gaze is the lead
• Don't smile: kata is danced with a neutral face
• Rehearse in your hakama - it hides the feet and changes your step length
• Practise in front of a mirror, counting aloud
• End on zanshin and hold it: the stillness is the applause cue [6]
What backs it up
In kata the uchidachi leads and the shidachi follows. The leader sets the tempo and invites each figure; a good follower never anticipates the lead, and answers it on the very next count.

The three most common errors: rushing the approach, letting the left heel drop, and losing the connection at the tips of the shinai. Each one breaks the line of dance.
